opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core of it stays the same, and that's deliberate. A lot of the value comes from asking the same questions in roughly the same way over time, so you can see how researchers' views shift. If we redesigned it every round, we'd lose that. So I'm fairly conservative about the main questions: when people expect high-level machine intelligence, when various occupations might be automated, and how likely people think different outcomes are, including extremely bad ones.

That said, there are things I'd like to improve or add.

One is dealing with framing effects more directly. We've seen that how you ask about timelines makes a big difference. Ask "in what year will there be a 50% chance?" versus "what's the probability by year X?" and you get noticeably different answers. Asking about "all tasks" versus "all occupations" also gives strikingly different answers, even though those should be about the same. I don't think that means the survey is useless. It tells you people haven't settled on precise views, and that's important to know. But I'd like to understand those inconsistencies better, maybe by asking people to reconcile their answers, or by testing which framings are most stable.

Another is more questions about specific, nearer-term milestones and concrete capabilities. Things are moving fast, so it's useful to have predictions that resolve within a few years. That lets us check how calibrated the field has been, and it's more grounded than asking only about something as abstract as "human-level AI."

I'd also like to ask more about the reasoning behind people's answers. When someone says there's a 10% chance of something catastrophic, what are they picturing? Is it misuse, loss of control, a slow erosion of human influence? What would change their mind? The numbers get a lot of attention, but the reasons behind them are probably more useful for working out what to do.

There's a practical side too. Response rates matter, and so does who's in the sample. We've mostly surveyed people who publish at top machine learning conferences. That's a reasonable population, but the field is changing. A lot of the most consequential work now happens inside companies that don't publish as much. So I'd like to think about how to include the views of people building frontier systems without losing comparability with earlier years.

And finally, I'd like to run it more often if possible. When the field changes this quickly, a gap of a year or two is a long time. More frequent snapshots would show whether views move with particular events, like big model releases, or whether they drift more slowly.

Overall the aim isn't to treat the survey as an oracle. AI researchers aren't necessarily expert forecasters, and the inconsistencies show that. But they're the people closest to the technology. It matters what they collectively believe, and especially whether a meaningful fraction of them take serious risks seriously. Tracking that carefully over time seems worthwhile.

r001.rationale: The response says keeping the same questions in roughly the same way lets researchers track how views shift over time, identifying comparability as the reason to preserve continuity.

r002.rationale: The response proposes adding topics and questions to the survey itself; it does not suggest using separate surveys for additional topics.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the main thing I'd want to do differently is actually ask less, in a sense, and ask more carefully. One thing we've learned from running it a few times is that the answers people give depend a lot on exactly how you frame the question. The most famous example is that if you ask about "high-level machine intelligence," where machines can do every task better and more cheaply than humans, people give you one date, and if you ask about "full automation of labor," where every occupation is fully automatable, they give you a date decades later. Those are, as far as I can tell, roughly the same thing described in two ways, and the gap between the answers is enormous. So that tells you that a lot of what you're measuring is framing effects, not stable beliefs.

I think the way to respond to that is partly to keep asking both versions, so you can at least track how the framing effect itself changes over time, rather than pretending one of them is the real number. But also to spend more effort on questions where the framing is less likely to matter, or where you can triangulate. Asking about specific, concrete milestones has been useful for that, because people seem to have somewhat more grounded intuitions about "when will an AI be able to write a New York Times bestseller" than about abstract definitions of general intelligence. Although even there, people have been consistently surprised. Many of the milestones were hit much earlier than the median forecast, which is itself interesting data about how much to trust the forecasts at all.

Another thing I'd like to do more of is just keep it consistent. The value of a survey like this compounds over time. A single snapshot of what researchers think is somewhat interesting, but the change between 2016, 2022, and 2023 is much more interesting, and that only works if you ask the same questions the same way. So there's a real tension between improving the survey and preserving comparability, and I've come to lean toward preserving comparability for the core questions and adding new things at the margin.

On the new things, I think I'd want to ask more about what people think should happen, not just what will happen. We did a bit of that, asking how much priority society should put on AI safety research, and whether people favored slowing down. And I'd like to understand the disagreement better. When you have a field where a large fraction of people put something like five percent or more on extremely bad outcomes, including human extinction, and another large fraction puts it near zero, the interesting question is why. What are they actually disagreeing about? Is it about how capable the systems will get, or how controllable they are, or about what humans will do with them? I don't think we've really gotten at that yet, and I think follow-up questions, or even interviews with a subset, could help.

And then the last thing, which is more mundane, is response rates and who's responding. We've gotten around fifteen percent, which is fine for this kind of thing but still leaves room to wonder whether the people who respond are different from the people who don't. We've looked at that a bit and haven't found big differences on the dimensions we can check, but I'd like to do more to make the sample as representative as possible, maybe by expanding the set of venues we draw from, since the field has gotten so much bigger and more spread out than when we started with just NeurIPS and ICML.

r001.rationale: The response says survey comparisons over time require asking the same questions the same way, and favors preserving comparability for core questions across editions.

r002.rationale: It proposes adding new topics at the margin and using follow-up questions or interviews; it does not propose separate surveys.

astra-6.text:
I think I would want to focus more on understanding what people mean by their answers. If someone gives a date for human-level AI, there are a lot of different pictures they might have in mind. And it matters whether those pictures differ, or whether people are imagining roughly the same thing and disagreeing about when it will happen.

So I’d be interested in doing more interviews alongside the survey, where you can ask follow-up questions: What do you expect the transition to look like? What would change your mind? How does this answer fit with your answers to the other questions?

There’s also a trade-off between improving the questions and keeping them consistent so we can track changes over time. I’d probably want a stable core of questions, with room to experiment around that. The aim would be to understand people’s uncertainty and reasoning, rather than just produce another median date.

r001.rationale: The response favors a stable core to track changes, but does not say future surveys should be identical to earlier editions; it also allows room to experiment.

r002.rationale: It proposes interviews alongside the survey, but does not propose separate surveys for additional topics or say to avoid expanding the existing survey.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d probably start by asking which questions we most want the survey to help us answer. There’s a temptation to keep adding questions, but researchers have limited time, and a longer survey can make it harder to get a representative set of responses.

I’d want to preserve some core questions so we can track changes over time, while experimenting with how we ask them. If you ask about essentially the same milestone in different ways and get quite different forecasts, that’s something you want to understand before putting too much weight on a particular number.

And I’d be interested in getting more of the reasoning behind people’s answers. What do they think is the main obstacle to more capable AI? What evidence would change their forecast? That could help us understand disagreements, rather than just reporting a distribution of dates.

r001.rationale: It recommends keeping some core questions for tracking changes, but also experimenting with how they are asked; it does not say to keep future editions identical to earlier ones.

r002.rationale: It notes drawbacks to adding questions but does not propose investigating additional topics in separate surveys.
